name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER_9_DIAGRAM_MCQ_Q01 - Electrodes and band migration in agarose gel electrophoresis

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the migration and separation of DNA fragments in an agarose gel electrophoresis apparatus under an applied electric field:

Which one of the following options correctly identifies the electrodes X and Y, and describes the relative molecular size of DNA fragments in bands A and B?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions:
The schematic diagram depicts an agarose gel slab with sample loading wells on one end and two electrodes X and Y at opposite ends. Band A is located closest to the loading wells, while Band B has migrated the farthest distance across the gel matrix.

Step 2: Assumptions and Physical/Biological Principles:
DNA molecules carry a net negative charge due to the presence of negatively charged phosphate groups in their sugar-phosphate backbone. When placed under an electric field, negatively charged DNA fragments migrate away from the negative electrode (cathode) toward the positive electrode (anode). The agarose matrix provides a molecular sieving effect, where resistance to movement is proportional to fragment size; consequently, smaller fragments move faster and travel farther than larger ones.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working and Deduction:
1. Since samples are loaded into wells near electrode X and migrate toward electrode Y, electrode X must be the negative terminal, known as the cathode (−).
2. Electrode Y, toward which the negatively charged fragments are attracted, must be the positive terminal, known as the anode (+).
3. Band A has experienced the least migration from the wells because larger DNA fragments face greater resistance through the agarose pores; thus, Band A represents the largest DNA fragments.
4. Band B has migrated the maximum distance toward the anode because smaller DNA fragments pass through the gel meshwork with higher mobility; thus, Band B represents the smallest DNA fragments.

Step 4: Check and Plausibility:
Verifying with electrophoretic laws confirms that cathode is negative, anode is positive, and fragment displacement is inversely proportional to the logarithm of molecular size.

Step 5: Final Conclusion:
Terminal X is the cathode (−), Terminal Y is the anode (+), Band A contains the largest DNA fragments, and Band B contains the smallest DNA fragments.

answer.text: X is Anode (+), Y is Cathode (−); Band A represents the smallest DNA fragments and Band B represents the largest DNA fragments.
X is Cathode (−), Y is Anode (+); Band A represents the smallest DNA fragments and Band B represents the largest DNA fragments.
X is Cathode (−), Y is Anode (+); Band A represents the largest DNA fragments and Band B represents the smallest DNA fragments.
X is Anode (+), Y is Cathode (−); Band A represents the largest DNA fragments and Band B represents the smallest DNA fragments.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER_9_DIAGRAM_MCQ_Q02 - Sequential steps and key enzyme in polymerase chain reaction

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents the three sequential steps of a single cycle of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR):

Which of the following correctly identifies Step I, Step II, Step III, and Enzyme X?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions:
The visual layout shows three ordered steps of a single thermal cycle in PCR starting with one double-stranded DNA template and ending with two synthesized double-stranded DNA molecules.

Step 2: Assumptions and Molecular Principles:
In vitro enzymatic amplification of DNA by Polymerase Chain Reaction involves three sequential temperature-dependent stages: 1. Denaturation of hydrogen bonds holding the two antiparallel template strands together. 2. Annealing of two sets of chemically synthesized oligonucleotide primers complementary to the 3′ flanking regions of the target sequence. 3. Extension of the primers along the template strands in the 5′ → 3′ direction by a thermostable DNA polymerase using deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working and Identification:
• In Step I, thermal energy (around 94–96°C) breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs to yield separated single template strands; this step is Denaturation.
• In Step II, cooling the reaction allows the synthetic primers to hybridize to their complementary sequences on each single strand; this step is Annealing.
• In Step III, the reaction temperature is raised to approximately 72°C where DNA polymerase synthesizes new complementary strands by adding nucleotides to the 3′-OH ends of the annealed primers; this step is Extension.
• Enzyme X must remain stable and catalytic through the high-temperature denaturation phase; hence, it is Taq polymerase, a thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus.

Step 4: Check and Plausibility:
Conventional DNA polymerases (such as E. coli DNA polymerase) would denature and lose all catalytic activity at 94°C, requiring replenishment every cycle. The use of thermostable Taq polymerase is essential for continuous automated thermal cycling.

Step 5: Final Conclusion:
Step I is Denaturation, Step II is Annealing, Step III is Extension, and Enzyme X is Taq polymerase.

answer.text: Step I: Denaturation; Step II: Annealing; Step III: Extension; Enzyme X: Taq polymerase
Step I: Annealing; Step II: Denaturation; Step III: Extension; Enzyme X: DNA ligase
Step I: Denaturation; Step II: Extension; Step III: Annealing; Enzyme X: RNA polymerase
Step I: Extension; Step II: Annealing; Step III: Denaturation; Enzyme X: Exonuclease

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER_9_DIAGRAM_MCQ_Q03 - Identification of restriction sites and functional regions in pBR322

questiontext.text:
The diagram below shows the circular cloning vector pBR322 with several annotated functional regions and restriction endonuclease recognition sites:

Which one of the following combinations correctly identifies the restriction site W located in the ampR gene, the restriction site X located in the tetR gene, and the functional regions Y and Z?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions:
The visual layout depicts the standard plasmid cloning vector pBR322 with labeled restriction recognition sites W (in ampR) and X (in tetR), as well as two essential chromosomal/plasmid maintenance regions labeled Y and Z at the lower hemisphere of the vector.

Step 2: Assumptions and Vector Architecture:
In the cloning vector pBR322: 1. The ampicillin resistance gene (ampR) contains unique recognition sequences for PstI and PvuI. 2. The tetracycline resistance gene (tetR) contains unique recognition sequences for BamHI and SalI. 3. The origin of replication (ori) controls autonomous plasmid replication and copy number. 4. The rop gene encodes proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid and contains a recognition site for PvuII.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working and Evaluation:
• Site W lies within the ampR coding segment; among common restriction enzymes, PstI cleaves specifically inside ampR.
• Site X lies within the tetR coding segment; BamHI cleaves specifically inside tetR.
• Region Y is situated adjacent to the lower-left sector, representing ori (origin of replication).
• Region Z is situated at the lower-right sector, representing rop (repressor of primer, which encodes proteins participating in plasmid replication).

Step 4: Check and Plausibility:
Inserting foreign DNA at Site X (BamHI) inactivates the tetracycline resistance gene, allowing selection of recombinants via ampicillin resistance and tetracycline sensitivity. This confirms that Site X is BamHI and Site W is PstI.

Step 5: Final Conclusion:
Site W is PstI, Site X is BamHI, Region Y is ori, and Region Z is rop.

answer.text: Site W: BamHI; Site X: PstI; Region Y: rop; Region Z: ori
Site W: SalI; Site X: PvuI; Region Y: ori; Region Z: rop
Site W: EcoRI; Site X: HindIII; Region Y: rop; Region Z: ori
Site W: PstI; Site X: BamHI; Region Y: ori; Region Z: rop

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER_9_DIAGRAM_MCQ_Q04 - Functional comparison of stirred-tank and sparged bioreactors

questiontext.text:
The schematics below illustrate two types of bioreactors employed for large-scale culture of recombinant microorganisms:

Based on the structural design and engineering principles of these bioreactors, which of the following statements provides the most accurate functional analysis of Feature I, Feature II, and Feature III?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions:
The visual layout contrasts two configurations of aerobic stirred bioreactors: (a) a simple stirred-tank reactor showing a curved base (Feature I) and multiple impeller blades (Feature II), and (b) a sparged stirred-tank reactor showing a perforated sparger delivery tube (Feature III) releasing micro-bubbles of sterile air throughout the broth.

Step 2: Assumptions and Biochemical Engineering Principles:
1. In high-density aerobic microbial cultures, oxygen has very low solubility in water, making oxygen transfer the primary rate-limiting factor for cell metabolism and recombinant protein yield.
2. Agitation must provide homogeneous mixing of nutrients, buffer chemicals, and dissolved gases without generating stagnant dead zones.
3. Bubble sparging increases the gas-liquid interfacial contact area, significantly accelerating the oxygen mass transfer rate into the liquid medium.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Functional Evaluation:
• Feature I (Curved reactor base): A cylindrical reactor with a curved or hemispherical bottom prevents the accumulation of culture broth in corners (dead zones) and promotes smooth recirculating hydrodynamic flow when driven by the central agitator.
• Feature II (Impeller blades): Rotating flat-bladed impellers break up large eddies, ensure continuous circulation of cells and substrates, and promote uniform dissolved oxygen availability throughout the large culture volume (100–1000 liters).
• Feature III (Sterile air sparger): Air bubbled through fine sparger nozzles creates millions of small gas bubbles; this dramatically increases the total surface area per unit volume available for oxygen transfer across the gas-liquid boundary layer into the culture broth.

Step 4: Check and Plausibility:
Alternative claims—such as Feature I serving solely to collect precipitated recombinant protein or Feature III serving for temperature control—are biologically and technically invalid. Recombinant proteins are produced throughout the culture broth and purified downstream, while temperature is maintained via an external heating/cooling jacket.

Step 5: Final Conclusion:
Feature I facilitates smooth mixing and avoids dead zones; Feature II ensures even nutrient mixing and oxygen availability; and Feature III dramatically increases the gas-liquid surface area for oxygen transfer via sterile air bubbling.

answer.text: Feature I serves to collect precipitated recombinant proteins at the bottom; Feature II delivers steam for in situ sterilization; Feature III removes toxic metabolic gases from the headspace.

Feature I facilitates smooth mixing and eliminates stagnant dead zones; Feature II ensures even mixing and oxygen distribution; Feature III dramatically increases the surface area for oxygen transfer via fine air bubbles.
Feature I provides structural insulation against temperature fluctuations; Feature II functions to lyse host cells after fermentation; Feature III delivers molten agar to solidify the culture medium.
Feature I facilitates continuous gravity drainage of the used medium; Feature II maintains high hydrostatic pressure; Feature III is a chemical port used exclusively for acid and base addition.
